en: The amihan is the cool northeast monsoon that brings dry weather to the Philippines from December to February.
The rich volcanic soil around Mount Mayon makes the surrounding Bicol region highly fertile for growing abaca plants.
The rocks in Zambales contain large deposits of chromite, a dark mineral used to make stainless steel.
Rainwater seeps into the limestone of Palawan to form the underground river at Puerto Princesa Subterranean River National Park.
Solar panels installed on rooftops in sunny Cebu convert light energy from the sun directly into electrical energy.
Filipino farmers traditionally plant rice when the Pleiades star cluster, locally called Moroporo, becomes visible in the night sky.
The gravitational pull of the moon causes the water level in Manila Bay to rise and fall twice daily.
When Mount Pinatubo erupted in 1991, it released massive amounts of ash and sulfur dioxide that temporarily cooled global temperatures.
The Valley Fault System is a massive crack in the Earth's crust that runs directly through the highly urbanized Metro Manila.
PAGASA declares an El Niño condition when sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, causing Philippine droughts.
The famous Chocolate Hills in Bohol are made of thousands of cone-shaped karst limestone mounds formed from ancient coral reefs.
Strong waves from frequent typhoons constantly erode the sandy coastal soil of vulnerable Pacific-facing islands like Eastern Samar.
